statement: A bus has 12 people on it. At the first stop, 5 get off and 3 get on. At the second stop, 4 get on. How many people got on at the two stops altogether?

choices.misconception: I counted only the people who got on at the second stop.
I added everyone who got off as well as everyone who got on, 5 + 3 + 4.
I worked out how many people are on the bus at the end, but the question asks how many got on.
I added every number in the story, 12, 5, 3 and 4.

hints: Read the last sentence again. What exactly is it asking about?
The question is not how many people are on the bus at the end. It asks only about people getting on. Decide which numbers you need before doing any adding.
3 people get on at the first stop and 4 get on at the second. The 12 and the 5 are not needed.

solutions.reliable: The question asks only how many people got on. At the first stop 3 got on and at the second stop 4 got on, and 3 + 4 = 7. The 12 people at the start and the 5 who got off do not matter. The idea to keep: decide which numbers the question needs before you start working.

whyOnTest: Finding what is actually asked: the story invites you to follow the whole bus ride, but the question is about one part of it.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
